verses.zh: 二人在以哥念同进犹太人的会堂，在那里讲的，叫犹太人和希腊人信的很多。
verses.en: The same thing happened in Iconium[NOTE:1] when Paul and Barnabas[NOTE:2] went into the Jewish synagogue[NOTE:3] and spoke in such a way that a large group[NOTE:4] of both Jews and Greeks believed.
notes: Iconium. See the note in 13:51.
Grk “they”; the referents (Paul and Barnabas) have been specified in the translation for clarity.
See the note on synagogue in 6:9.
Or “that a large crowd.”
verses.commentary:
14:1 "Iconium" There is a second century non-canonical book known as The Acts of Paul and
Thekla, which is reported to be Paul's activities in Iconium. This book possibly contains the only
physical descriptions of Paul ever recorded: short, bald, bow legged, heavy eyebrows, and protruding eyes
(cf. 2 Cor. 10:10). It is quite uninspired and yet reflects the impact that the Apostle Paul had in this region of
Asia Minor. Most of this area was in the Roman Province of Galatia.

▣ "entered the synagogue" This was Paul and Barnabas' regular pattern (cf. Acts 9:20; 13:5,14; 14:1; 18:4,19;
Rom. 1:16). These hearers, both Jews and God-fearing Greeks, would be familiar with the OT prophecies and promises.

▣ "a large number of people believed, both of Jews and of Greeks" This phrase shows the purpose
of Acts. The gospel is spreading vigorously among various people groups. The implications of the OT promises
to all humanity (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:15; 12:3) are now being realized.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL
REDEMPTIVE PLAN

"Believe" is a major theological concept in Scripture. Remember, most NT authors (except Luke) were
Hebrew thinkers writing in Koine Greek. So, modern interpreters must seek the intended meaning in the Koine Greek
translation of the OT called the Septuagint, and not simply Greek lexicons.

These summary statements relating to the rapid growth of the church are characteristic of
Luke's writings. See "Introduction to Acts," "Purpose and Structure," #1,3.

verses.zh: 但那不顺从的犹太人耸动外邦人，叫他们心里恼恨弟兄。
verses.en: But the Jews who refused to believe[NOTE:1] stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds[NOTE:2] against the brothers.
notes: Or “who would not believe.”
Or “embittered their minds” (Grk “their souls”). BDAG 502 s.v. κακόω 2 has “make angry, embitter τὰς ψυχάς τινων κατά τινος poison the minds of some persons against another Ac 14:2.”
verses.commentary:
14:2 "the Jews who disbelieved" Salvation is characterized by "believed" (cf. Acts 14:1). Spiritual
blindness and recalcitrance is characterized by "disobedience" or "disbelief." The refusal to respond to
the gospel dooms one to blindness and lostness! See note at Acts 13:12 (second paragraph).

Luke documents the virulent antagonism of Jewish unbelief and active persecution. It is
their rejection that opens the door of faith to the Gentiles (cf. Romans 9-11). The focus of the NT is not Israel
and her future, but Jesus and the gospel. Be careful of reading the NT through the OT promises to Israel. The
revelation of Jesus changes everything!

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEWS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE UNPARDONABLE SIN

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN UNTO DEATH

▣ "stirred up" This is a common Septuagint VERB for rebellion
(cf. 1 Sam. 3:12; 22:8; 2 Sam. 18:31; 22:49; 1 Chr. 5:26), but it is used in the NT only in Acts 13:50
and here. Luke was greatly influenced by the terminology of the Septuagint.

▣ "embittered" This is another common term in the Septuagint to describe evil, oppressive
people who mistreat others. Luke uses this term often in Acts (cf. Acts 7:6,19; 12:1; 14:2; 18:10). Luke was
well familiar with the Septuagint.

verses.zh: 二人在那里住了多日，倚靠主放胆讲道；主藉他们的手施行神迹奇事，证明他的恩道。
verses.en: So they stayed there[NOTE:1] for a considerable time, speaking out courageously for the Lord, who testified[NOTE:2] to the message[NOTE:3] of his grace, granting miraculous signs[NOTE:4] and wonders to be performed through their hands.
notes: The word “there” is not in the Greek text, but is implied.
The Lord testified to the message by granting the signs described in the following clause.
Grk “word.”
Here the context indicates the miraculous nature of the signs mentioned.
verses.commentary:
14:3 God used the miraculous to confirm His gracious character and the truthfulness of the radically
new gospel of Jesus Christ in this New Age (cf. Acts 4:29-30; Heb. 2:4).

▣ "speaking boldly" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: BOLDNESS

verses.zh: 城里的众人就分了党，有附从犹太人的，有附从使徒的。
verses.en: But the population[NOTE:1] of the city was divided; some[NOTE:2] sided with the Jews, and some with the apostles.
notes: BDAG 825 s.v. πλῆθος 2.b.γ has this translation for πλῆθος (plēthos).
These clauses are a good example of the contrastive μὲν…δέ (men…de) construction: Some “on the one hand” sided with the Jews, but some “on the other hand” sided with the apostles.
verses.commentary:
14:4 "But the people of the city were divided" The word of truth always divides (cf. Acts 17:4-5; 19:9;
28:24; Matt. 10:34-36). Some of the Jews in the Synagogue believed, but others became militant against the
gospel. This is the mystery of wickedness! See note at Acts 13:12 (second paragraph).

▣ "with the apostles" This refers to both Paul and Barnabas. In this chapter (i.e., Acts 14:4
and 14) is the only time Luke uses this term to refer to anyone except the original Twelve. This is also implied
in 1 Cor. 9:5-6. This is obviously a wider use of the term "apostle" than the Twelve.

- James the Just (half brother of Jesus) is called an apostle in Galatians 1:19.

- Silvanus and Timothy were called apostles in 1 Thess. 1:1 combined with 2:6.

- Andronicus and Junius (Junia in KJV), are called apostles in Rom. 16:6-7.

- Apollos is called an apostle in 1 Cor. 4:6-9.

The twelve Apostles were unique. When they died no one replaced them (except Matthias
for Judas, cf. Acts 1). However there is an ongoing gift of apostleship mentioned in 1 Cor, 12:28 and
Eph. 4:11. The NT does not provide enough information to describe the functions of this gift or how to
know one has it.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEND (apostellō)

verses.zh: 那时，外邦人和犹太人，并他们的官长，一齐拥上来，要凌辱使徒，用石头打他们。
verses.en: When both the Gentiles and the Jews (together with their rulers) made[NOTE:1] an attempt to mistreat[NOTE:2] them and stone them,[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “So there came about an attempt” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
On this verb see BDAG 1022 s.v. ὑβρίζω.
The direct object “them” is repeated after both verbs in the translation for stylistic reasons, although it occurs only after λιθοβολῆσαι (lithobolēsai) in the Greek text.
verses.commentary:
14:5 "with their rulers" This could refer to the leaders of the city or the leaders of the synagogue.
Some early scribes and modern commentators assert two persecutions, (1) Acts 14:2 and (2) Acts 14:5, but
the context implies just one.

Again, one must notice that Luke clearly differentiated between local and Jewish trouble makers
and believers. Christianity was not a threat to Roman governmental authority.

NASB, NRSV, TEV
"mistreat"

NKJV
"abuse"

NJB
"make attacks"

REB
"maltreat"

Peshitta
"menaced"

The Greek term hubrizō is more intense than "mistreat," possibly "to
run riot," or "to commit violent acts." It is very common in the Septuagint. Luke uses this term often
in three senses.

- insult, Luke 11:45

- violent act, Luke 18:32; Acts 14:5

- loss of physical property, Acts 27:10,21

▣ "stone" This second descriptive term shows just how violently the opposition planned to
attack the believers. Paul mentions he was once stoned in 2 Cor. 11:25. Probably the Jewish element chose
this specific means because of its OT connection to blasphemy (i.e., Lev. 24:16; John 8:59; 10:31-33).

SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH

verses.zh: 使徒知道了，就逃往吕高尼的路司得、特庇两个城和周围地方去，
verses.en: Paul and Barnabas[NOTE:1] learned about it[NOTE:2] and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra[NOTE:3] and Derbe[NOTE:4] and the surrounding region.
notes: Grk “they”; the referents (Paul and Barnabas) have been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “learning about it, fled.” The participle συνιδόντες (sunidontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. It could also be taken temporally (“when they learned about it”) as long as opening clause of v. 5 is not translated as a temporal clause too, which results in a redundancy.

Lystra was a city in Lycaonia about 18 mi (30 km) south of Iconium, a Roman colony that was not on the main roads of Lycaonia. Because of its relative isolation, its local character was able to be preserved.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2.
Derbe was a city in Lycaonia about 35 mi (60 km) southeast of Lystra.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2.
verses.commentary:
14:6 "and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe" Iconium (v. 1) was in Phyrgia. It was close to
the boundary of a racially distinct group. This detail shows the historicity of the book of Acts.

The NET Bible (p. 2014, #23) mentions that these cities were not on a major road and that by
their isolation they were able to retain their cultural and linguistic heritage.

verses.zh: 在那里传福音。
verses.en: There[NOTE:1] they continued to proclaim[NOTE:2] the good news.
notes: Grk “region, and there.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, καί (kai) has not been translated and a new sentence begun in the translation.
The periphrastic construction εὐαγγελιζόμενοι ἦσαν (euangelizomenoi ēsan) has been translated as a progressive imperfect.
verses.commentary:
14:7 The VERB is a PERIPHRASTIC PERFECT MIDDLE, meaning that they
preached again and again. This is the theme of Paul's missionary journeys (cf. Acts 14:21; 16:10). Those
who trusted Christ under his preaching also sensed the urgency and mandate to present the gospel to
others. This was/is the priority (cf. Matt. 28:19-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8)!

verses.zh: 路司得城里坐着一个两脚无力的人，生来是瘸腿的，从来没有走过。
verses.en: In[NOTE:1] Lystra[NOTE:2] sat a man who could not use his feet,[NOTE:3] lame from birth,[NOTE:4] who had never walked.
notes: Grk “And in.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Lystra was a city in Lycaonia about 18 mi (30 km) south of Iconium.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2.
Grk “powerless in his feet,” meaning he was unable to use his feet to walk.

Grk “lame from his mother’s womb” (an idiom).sn The description lame from birth makes clear how serious the condition was, and how real it was. This event is very similar to Acts 3:1-10, except here the lame man’s faith is clear from the start.
verses.commentary:
14:8 "At Lystra" This town was Timothy's home (cf. Acts 16:1-2). This is a Roman colony established
by Augustus in A.D. 6. There was probably no synagogue here, so Paul and Barnabas conducted
street preaching.

▣ So that there was no possibility of a trick or deception (cf. Acts 3:2). There are three
specific descriptive phrases describing this man's permanent condition.

- no strength in his feet

- lame from his mother's womb

- had never walked

▣ "no strength" The term adunatos usually means "impossible" or literally "unable"
(cf. Luke 18:27; Heb. 6:4,18; 10:4; 11:6), but here Luke uses it like the medical writers in the sense
of impotent or weak (cf. Rom. 8:3; 15:1).

It is interesting that Luke, in many ways, shows the parallels between Peter's and Paul's ministries.
Peter and John heal a lame man in Acts 3:1-10 now so too, do Paul and Barnabas.

verses.zh: 他听保罗讲道，保罗定睛看他，见他有信心，可得痊愈，
verses.en: This man was listening to Paul as he was speaking. When Paul[NOTE:1] stared[NOTE:2] intently at him and saw he had faith to be healed,
notes: Grk “speaking, who.” The relative pronoun has been replaced by the noun “Paul,” and a new sentence begun in the translation because an English relative clause would be very awkward here.
Or “looked.”
verses.commentary:
14:9 "when he had fixed his gaze on him" Luke uses this phrase often (cf. Acts 3:4; 10:4). See note
at Acts 1:10. Paul saw that this man was listening intently. Therefore, he commanded him to stand up
and walk (cf. v 10) and he did!

▣ "that he had faith to be made well" "Well" is used in the OT sense of the term "saved," meaning
physical deliverance. Notice that Paul's ability to heal was based on the man's faith. This is often,
but not exclusively, the case in the NT (cf. Luke 5:20; John 5:5-9). Miracles had several functions:

- to show the love of God

- to show the power and truth of the gospel

- to train and encourage the other believers present

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FAITH

verses.zh: 就大声说：「你起来，两脚站直！」那人就跳起来，而且行走。
verses.en: he said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.”[NOTE:1] And the man[NOTE:2] leaped up and began walking.[NOTE:3]
notes: BDAG 722 s.v. ὀρθός 1.a has “stand upright on your feet.”
Grk “he”; the referent (the man) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
This verb is imperfect tense in contrast to the previous verb, which is aorist. It has been translated ingressively, since the start of a sequence is in view here.

verses.zh: 众人看见保罗所做的事，就用吕高尼的话大声说：「有　神藉着人形降临在我们中间了。」
verses.en: So when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they shouted[NOTE:1] in the Lycaonian language,[NOTE:2] “The gods have come down to us in human form!”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “they lifted up their voice” (an idiom).
Grk “in Lycaonian, saying.” The word “language” is not in the Greek text, but is implied. The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in English and has not been translated.

So BDAG 707 s.v. ὁμοιόω 1. However, L&N 64.4 takes the participle ὁμοιωθέντες (homoiōthentes) as an adjectival participle modifying θεοί (theoi): “the gods resembling men have come down to us.”sn The gods have come down to us in human form. Greek culture spoke of “divine men.” In this region there was a story of Zeus and Hermes visiting the area (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.611-725). The locals failed to acknowledge them, so judgment followed. The present crowd was determined not to make the mistake a second time.
verses.commentary:
14:11 "in the Lycaonian language" Obviously Paul and Barnabas did not understand what the crowd was
saying. This was the indigenous language of the region.

verses.zh: 于是称巴拿巴为宙斯，称保罗为希耳米，因为他说话领首。
verses.en: They began to call[NOTE:1] Barnabas Zeus[NOTE:2] and Paul Hermes,[NOTE:3] because he was the chief speaker.
notes: The imperfect verb ἐκάλουν (ekaloun) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.
Zeus was the chief Greek deity, worshiped throughout the Greco-Roman world (known to the Romans as Jupiter).
Hermes was a Greek god who (according to Greek mythology) was the messenger of the gods and the god of oratory (equivalent to the Roman god Mercury).
verses.commentary:
14:12 "calling Barnabas Zeus and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker" A local tradition
asserted that the Greek gods visited humans in human form, but these cities did not recognize them and were
punished (cf. Ovid, Metamorphoses 8:626ff). From local inscriptions we learn this was an area where Zeus
(Roman Jupiter) and Hermes (Roman Mercury) were worshiped (cf. Acts 14:13).

Notice that Barnabas is mentioned first. This is probably because Paul, as the spokesperson,
would be understood by these pagans as the equivalent of Hermes (Mercury); the silent Barnabas must then
be the high god Zeus (Jupiter).

verses.zh: 有城外宙斯庙的祭司牵着牛，拿着花圈，来到门前，要同众人向使徒献祭。
verses.en: The priest of the temple[NOTE:1] of Zeus,[NOTE:2] located just outside the city, brought bulls[NOTE:3] and garlands[NOTE:4] to the city gates; he and the crowds wanted to offer sacrifices to them.[NOTE:5]
notes: The words “the temple of” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. The translation “the priest of (the temple/shrine of) Zeus located before the city” is given for this phrase by BDAG 426 s.v. Ζεύς.
See the note on Zeus in the previous verse.
Or “oxen.”

Or “wreaths.”sn Garlands were commonly wreaths of wool with leaves and flowers woven in, worn on a person’s head or woven around a staff. They were an important part of many rituals used to worship pagan gods. Although it was an erroneous reaction, the priest’s reaction shows how all acknowledged their power and access to God.
The words “to them” are not in the Greek text, but are clearly implied by the response of Paul and Barnabas in the following verse.
verses.commentary:
14:13 "gate" This could refer to the city or, more probably, to the temple of Jupiter (Zeus) which
was located just outside the city gate and facing it. It was a time of great confusion and misunderstanding.

verses.zh: 巴拿巴、保罗二使徒听见，就撕开衣裳，跳进众人中间，喊着说：
verses.en: But when the apostles[NOTE:1] Barnabas and Paul heard about[NOTE:2] it, they tore[NOTE:3] their clothes and rushed out[NOTE:4] into the crowd, shouting,[NOTE:5]
notes: The apostles Barnabas and Paul. This is one of only two places where Luke calls Paul an apostle, and the description here is shared with Barnabas. This is a nontechnical use here, referring to a commissioned messenger.
The participle ἀκούσαντες (akousantes) is taken temporally.

Grk “tearing their clothes they rushed out.” The participle διαρρήξαντες (diarrēxantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. This action is a Jewish response to blasphemy (m. Sanhedrin 7.5; Jdt 14:16-17).
So BDAG 307 s.v. ἐκπηδάω 1, “rush (lit. ‘leap’) out…εἰς τὸν ὄχλον into the crowd Ac 14:14.”

Grk “shouting and saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes, in v. 15) has not been translated because it is redundant.sn What follows is one of two speeches in Acts to a purely pagan audience (Acts 17 in Athens is the other). So Paul focused on God as Creator, a common link.
verses.commentary:
14:14 "apostles" See full note at Acts 14:4.

▣ "Barnabas" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: BARNABAS

▣ "tore their robes" This is a Jewish sign of mourning and blasphemy (cf. Matt. 26:65;
Mark 14:63; and note in Talmud tractates Sanhedrin 7.5). It surely would have communicated even to these
pagans that there was a problem.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "rushed out" This is a common term in the Septuagint for "leaping out" or "rushing out,"
though it is used only here in the NT. Paul and Barnabas sprang up and out into the midst of the crowd.

verses.zh: 「诸君，为甚么做这事呢？我们也是人，性情和你们一样。我们传福音给你们，是叫你们离弃这些虚妄，归向那创造天、地、海，和其中万物的永生　神。
verses.en: “Men, why are you doing these things? We too are men, with human natures[NOTE:1] just like you! We are proclaiming the good news to you, so that you should turn[NOTE:2] from these worthless[NOTE:3] things to the living God, who made the heaven, the earth,[NOTE:4] the sea, and everything that is in them.
notes: Grk “with the same kinds of feelings,” L&N 25.32. BDAG 706 s.v. ὁμοιοπαθής translates the phrase “with the same nature τινί as someone.” In the immediate context, the contrast is between human and divine nature, and the point is that Paul and Barnabas are mere mortals, not gods.

Grk “in order that you should turn,” with ἐπιστρέφειν (epistrephein) as an infinitive of purpose, but this is somewhat awkward contemporary English. To translate the infinitive construction “proclaim the good news, that you should turn,” which is much smoother English, could give the impression that the infinitive clause is actually the content of the good news, which it is not. The somewhat less formal “to get you to turn” would work, but might convey to some readers manipulativeness on the part of the apostles. Thus “proclaim the good news, so that you should turn,” is used, to convey that the purpose of the proclamation of good news is the response by the hearers. The emphasis here is like 1 Thess 1:9-10.
Or “useless,” “futile.” The reference is to idols and idolatry, worshiping the creation over the Creator (Rom 1:18-32). See also 1 Kgs 16:2, 13, 26; 2 Kgs 17:15; Jer 2:5; 8:19; 3 Macc 6:11.

Grk “and the earth, and the sea,” but καί (kai) has not been translated before “the earth” and “the sea” since contemporary English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.
verses.commentary:
14:15-17 Here is a summary of Paul's first sermon to pagans. It is much like his sermon on Mars
Hill (cf. Acts 17:22-33).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE
EARLY CHURCH

14:15

NASB, NKJV
"men of the same nature as you"

NRSV
"we are mortals just like you"

TEV
"we ourselves are only human beings like you"

NJB
"We are only human beings, mortal like yourselves"

REB
"We are human beings, just like you"

Peshitta
"We are also ordinary human beings like you"

The term is homoiopathēs, which is a compound of "the same" and "passions."
This term is used only here and in James 5:17 in the NT. The locals had thought Paul and Barnabas were
gods (homoiōthentes, cf. Acts 14:11), which means "made like" men. Paul uses the same root
to denote their common humanity. Luke shows the humility of Paul and Barnabas in contradistinction to
Herod Antipas in Acts 12:20-23.

▣ "that you should turn" Repentance in the OT is characterized by

- a turning from idols and sin (cf. 1 Thess. 1:9)

- a turning to God (i.e., faith and faithfulness)

Both of these are required for a biblical salvation!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE IN THE NT

▣ "from these vain things" The term "vain" means empty, void, non-existent.
Paul is directly confronting their superstitious paganism. The Bible contrasts the one true creator God with the
man-made idols (i.e., human superstition based on natural events or animals, cf. Rom. 1:18-32). There are
several different words and phrases used, but all communicate the same concept of "nothingness." Here are
a few sample texts.

- from the Ten Commandments ‒ Exod. 20:4; Deut. 5:8 (also note 4:15-19,25,28; 27:15)

- problem with the golden calf ‒ Exodus 32

- from Leviticus ‒ cf. Lev. 19:4; 26:1)

- from the history books of the OT

- 1 Sam. 12:21-22

- 1 Kgs. 15:30 (the two golden calves); 16:13,26

- 2 Kgs. 17:15; 19:18

- from the Psalms ‒ Ps. 31:6; 115:2-8; 135:15-18

- from the major prophets

- Isa. 2:8; 17:8; 41:24,29; 44:9-20

- Jer. 2:5; 8:19; 10:2-5; 14:22

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: VAIN, EMPTY, NOTHINGNESS

▣ "to a living God" This is a play on the name YHWH, which is a form of the Hebrew
VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3:14). YHWH is the ever-living, only-living God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "who made" This is a quote Exod. 20:11 or Ps. 146:6. The
Hebrew term Elohim (cf. Gen. 1:1) describes God as creator and provider (cf. The Expositor's
Bible Commentary, vol. 1, pp. 468-469) as YHWH describes Him as Savior, Redeemer (cf. Gen. 2:4, i.e., The
Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 1, pp. 471-472) and covenant-making God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. (Elohim) and D. (YHWH)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

verses.zh: 他在从前的世代，任凭万国各行其道；
verses.en: In[NOTE:1] past[NOTE:2] generations he allowed all the nations[NOTE:3] to go their own ways,
notes: Grk “them, who in.” The relative pronoun (“who”) was replaced by the pronoun “he” (“In past generations he”) and a new sentence was begun in the translation at this point to improve the English style, due to the length of the sentence in Greek and the awkwardness of two relative clauses (“who made the heaven” and “who in past generations”) following one another.
On this term see BDAG 780 s.v. παροίχομαι. The word is a NT hapax legomenon.
Or “all the Gentiles” (in Greek the word for “nation” and “Gentile” is the same). The plural here alludes to the variety of false religions in the pagan world.
verses.commentary:
14:16 "In the generations gone by He permitted all the nations to go their own ways" This phrase may
be an allusion to Deut. 32:7-8 (LXX) in which Moses asserts that YHWH establishes the boundaries of the nations.
Theologically this affirms God's care and attention to all nations (Gentiles, cf. Girdlestone, Synonyms
of the Old Testament, pp. 258-259). God desired that they know Him, but the fallenness of humanity
caused superstition and idolatry (cf. Rom. 1:18-2:29). However, He continued to pursue them (cf. Acts 14:17).

The Gentile's ignorance of God is contrasted with the Jews' knowledge of God. The irony is
that Gentiles respond in mass by faith to the gospel, while Jews respond in mass rejection and persecution
toward the gospel (cf. Romans 9-11).

verses.zh: 然而为自己未尝不显出证据来，就如常施恩惠，从天降雨，赏赐丰年，叫你们饮食饱足，满心喜乐。」
verses.en: yet he did not leave himself without a witness by doing good,[NOTE:1] by giving you rain from heaven[NOTE:2] and fruitful seasons, satisfying you[NOTE:3] with food and your hearts with joy.”[NOTE:4]
notes: The participle ἀγαθουργῶν (agathourgōn) is regarded as indicating means here, parallel to the following participles διδούς (didous) and ἐμπιπλῶν (empiplōn). This is the easiest way to understand the Greek structure. Semantically, the first participle is a general statement, followed by two participles giving specific examples of doing good.
Or “from the sky” (the same Greek word means both “heaven” and “sky”).

Grk “satisfying [filling] your hearts with food and joy.” This is an idiomatic expression; it strikes the English reader as strange to speak of “filling one’s heart with food.” Thus the additional direct object “you” has been supplied, separating the two expressions somewhat: “satisfying you with food and your hearts with joy.”

God’s general sovereignty and gracious care in the creation are the way Paul introduces the theme of the goodness of God. He was trying to establish monotheism here. It is an OT theme (Gen 8:22; Pss 4:7; 145:15-16; 147:8-9; Isa 25:6; Jer 5:24) which also appears in the NT (Luke 12:22-34).
verses.commentary:
14:17 "He did not leave Himself without witness" This is the concept of natural revelation
(cf. Ps. 19:1-6; Rom. 1:19-20). All humans know something about God from creation and an inner
moral witness (cf. Rom. 2:14-15).

▣ "rains. . .food" The local pagan tradition said that Zeus was the giver of rain and Hermes
was the giver of food. Paul, following Deuteronomy 27-29 (and also Jesus in Matt. 5:45), affirms God's control of nature.

These pagans did not know YHWH so the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 are replaced by God's
patience (cf. Acts 17:30; Rom. 3:25; 4:15; 5:13). Paul was God's unique choice (Apostle to the Gentiles, cf. Acts 9)
to reach the nations! Paul uses God's creation and provision through nature (cf. Ps. 145:15-16; 147:8;
Jer. 5:24; Jonah 1:9) as his point of contact.

It is interesting that there is nothing of the gospel per se recorded by Luke in this sermon summary. One
assumes that Paul continued in the same line of reasoning as he did in his Athenian sermon in Acts 17:16-34.
One wonders whether Luke got this summary from Paul or possibly Timothy (this was his home).

verses.zh: 二人说了这些话，仅仅地拦住众人不献祭与他们。
verses.en: Even by saying[NOTE:1] these things, they scarcely persuaded[NOTE:2] the crowds not to offer sacrifice to them.

BDAG 524 s.v. καταπαύω 2.b gives both “restrain” and “dissuade someone fr. someth.,” but “they scarcely dissuaded the crowds from offering sacrifice,” while accurate, is less common in contemporary English than saying “they scarcely persuaded the crowds not to offer sacrifice.” Paganism is portrayed as a powerful reality that is hard to reverse.
verses.commentary: 14:18 This is an eyewitness detail.

verses.zh: 但有些犹太人从安提阿和以哥念来，挑唆众人，就用石头打保罗，以为他是死了，便拖到城外。
verses.en: But Jews came from Antioch[NOTE:1] and Iconium,[NOTE:2] and after winning[NOTE:3] the crowds over, they stoned[NOTE:4] Paul and dragged him out of the city, presuming him to be dead.
notes: Antioch was a city in Pisidia about 90 mi (145 km) west northwest of Lystra.map For location see JP1-E2; JP2-E2; JP3-E2; JP4-E2.
Iconium was a city in Lycaonia about 18 mi (30 km) north of Lystra. Note how Jews from other cities were chasing Paul (2 Cor 11:4-6; Gal 2:4-5; Acts 9:16).
The participle πείσαντες (peisantes) is taken temporally (BDAG 791 s.v. πείθω 1.c).
Grk “stoning Paul they dragged him.” The participle λιθάσαντες (lithasantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
verses.commentary:
14:19 Jewish opposition in the cities where Paul had preached united in recurrent attacks on him
(cf. 2 Cor. 4:7-15; 6:3-10; 11:23-30). Notice that the attack was focused on Paul, not Barnabas. Notice
also the fickleness of the pagan crowd. Paul and Barnabas are honored as gods one moment and stoned the next!

▣ "they stoned Paul" This was not a resuscitation miracle, but an account of Paul's physical
stamina and bravery (cf. Acts 14:20-21). 2 Corinthians 11:25 and Galatians 6:17 also refer to this same
event. The stoning planned in Acts 14:5 now became a reality!

a prayer meeting to which God wondrously responded. Notice how persecution continued to be the

14:21 "After they had preached the gospel to that city" This refers to Derbe (cf. Acts 14:20). This

This city also wonderfully responded to the gospel and many were saved.

▣ "they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch" Apparently they did not preach publicly
on this return visit, but were privately organizing and encouraging the believers (cf. Acts 14:22-23).

verses.zh: 坚固门徒的心，劝他们恒守所信的道；又说：「我们进入　神的国，必须经历许多艰难。」
verses.en: They strengthened[NOTE:1] the souls of the disciples and encouraged them to continue[NOTE:2] in the faith, saying, “We must enter the kingdom of God[NOTE:3] through many persecutions.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “to Antioch, strengthening.” Due to the length of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English to use shorter sentences, a new sentence was started here. This participle (ἐπιστηρίζοντες, epistērizontes) and the following one (παρακαλοῦντες, parakalountes) have been translated as finite verbs connected by the coordinating conjunction “and.”
And encouraged them to continue. The exhortations are like those noted in Acts 11:23; 13:43. An example of such a speech is found in Acts 20:18-35. Christianity is now characterized as “the faith.”

This reference to the kingdom of God clearly refers to its arrival as future, although this does not automatically rule out a present manifestation of the kingdom as well. The nature of the kingdom of God in the NT and in Jesus’ teaching has long been debated by interpreters and scholars, with discussion primarily centering around the nature of the kingdom (earthly, heavenly, or both) and the kingdom’s arrival (present, future, or both). An additional major issue concerns the relationship between the kingdom of God and the person and work of Jesus himself. See Luke 6:20; 11:20; 17:20-21; Acts 1:3.
Or “sufferings.”
verses.commentary:
14:22 This verse is a summary of Paul's discipleship message. Notice it is focused on (1) perseverance
and (2) tribulation. Believers are matured through the expected trials (cf. John 15:18,20; 16:33; Rom. 5:3-4; 8:17-18;
1 Thess. 3:3; 2 Tim. 3:12; James 1:2-4; 1 Pet. 4:12-16; Rev. 1:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

▣ "strengthening" This term is used several times in the Septuagint in the sense of "to cause
to rest on" or "to be established." Luke uses this term several times to describe Paul's follow-up discipleship
ministry (cf. Acts 11:26; 14:28; 15:32,41; 18:23; 20:18ff).

▣ "the souls of the disciples" The term soul (psuchē) is used in the sense of
the person or their mental activities. This is not the Greek concept of every person having an immortal
soul, but the Hebrew concept of soul (nephesh, BDB 659, KB 711-713, cf. Gen. 2:7, see full note online) as a way of
referring to a human being (cf. Acts 2:41; 3:23; 7:14; 14:2,22; 15:24; 27:37).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

SPECIAL TOPIC: BODY AND SPIRIT

▣ "encouraging them to continue in the faith" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Acts 11:23; 13:43).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NEED TO PERSEVERE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FAITH

▣ "the kingdom of God" This is a difficult phrase to interpret. Jesus used it often in connection
to His own ministry. However, the Apostles obviously misunderstood its significance (cf. Acts 1:3,6). In
Acts it is almost synonymous with the gospel (cf. Acts 8:12; 19:8; 20:25; 28:23,31).

It is this "already" (cf. Matt. 12:28; Luke 16:16) vs. "not yet" (cf. Matt. 24:14,30,36-37; 25:30,31;
2 Pet. 1:11) tension which characterizes this age. The Kingdom has come in Jesus Christ (i.e., First Coming), but its
consummation is future (i.e., Second Coming).

verses.zh: 二人在各教会中选立了长老，又禁食祷告，就把他们交托所信的主。
verses.en: When they had appointed elders[NOTE:1] for them in the various churches,[NOTE:2] with prayer and fasting[NOTE:3] they entrusted them to the protection[NOTE:4] of the Lord in whom they had believed.
notes: Appointed elders. See Acts 20:17.
The preposition κατά (kata) is used here in a distributive sense; see BDAG 512 s.v. κατά B.1.d.

Literally with a participle (προσευξάμενοι, proseuxamenoi) rather than a noun, “praying with fasting,” but the combination “prayer and fasting” is so familiar in English that it is preferable to use it here.

BDAG 772 s.v. παρατίθημι 3.b has “entrust someone to the care or protection of someone” for this phrase. The reference to persecution or suffering in the context (v. 22) suggests “protection” is a better translation here. This looks at God’s ultimate care for the church.
verses.commentary:
14:23 "they had appointed elders" The term "elders" (presbuteros) is synonymous with the terms
"bishop" (episkopos) and "pastors" (poimenos) in the NT (cf. Acts 20:17,28 and Titus 1:5,7; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: ELDERS).
The term "elder" has a Jewish background (cf. Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, pp. 244-246
and Frank Stagg, New Testament Theology, pp. 262-264), while the term "bishop" or "overseer" has a
Greek city-state background. There are only two church officers listed in the NT: pastors and deacons
(cf. Phil. 1:1).

The term "appoint" can mean "elect by the show of hands" (cf. 2 Cor. 8:19 and Louw and Nida,
Greek-English Lexicon, pp. 363, 484). The term is later used of "ordination" by the early church
fathers. The real issue is how does "elect by vote" fit this context? A vote by these new churches seems
inappropriate (although the church in Jerusalem voted for the Seven in Acts 6 and the church votes to affirm
Paul's ministry to the Gentiles in Acts 15).

F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, p. 79 says, "originally indicated appointment
or election by a show of hands (literally by stretching out the hand), it had lost this specific force
by New Testament times and had come to mean simply 'appoint,' no matter by what procedure." One cannot
advocate or reject an ecclesiastical polity by the use of this term in the NT.

Notice that Paul instructs Titus to also appoint "elders" on Crete, but to Timothy in
Ephesus Paul says let the church select persons with certain qualifications (cf. 1 Timothy 3). In new
areas leaders were appointed, but in established areas leadership traits had a chance to be manifested
and be affirmed by the local church.

Notice that Paul's missionary strategy is to establish local churches who will continue
the task of evangelism and discipleship in their area (cf. Matt. 28:19-20). This is God's method for
reaching the entire world (i.e., local churches)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH POLITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: ORDINATION

▣ "church" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH (ekklēsia)

▣ "having prayed with fasting" This may be purposefully parallel to Acts 13:2-3. Paul had experienced
the Spirit's power and direction at Antioch. He continued this same spiritual pattern. They had to prepare
themselves for God to reveal His will.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EFFECTIVE PRAYER

SPECIAL TOPIC: FASTING

▣ "in whom they had believed" This is a PLUPERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE
which denotes a settled action in past time. These new elders had believed for a period of time and had proved
to be faithful, exhibiting leadership qualities.

This grammatical construction of eis connected to pisteuō (cf. Acts 10:43)
is characteristic of John's writings (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: JOHN'S USE
OF THE VERB "BELIEVE"), but is also present in Paul's writings(cf. Rom. 10:14; Gal. 2:16; Phil. 1:29)
and Peter's (cf. 1 Pet. 1:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FAITH, BELIEVE, or
TRSUT

▣ "they commended them to the Lord" This does not refer to some type of ordination. The
same VERB is used in Acts 14:26 of Paul and Barnabas, while in Acts 20:32 for those who
were already elders. Ordination is helpful in that it emphasizes the truth that God calls people into
leadership roles. It is a negative and unbiblical if it makes a distinction between believers. All
believers are called and gifted for ministry (cf. Eph. 4:11-12). There is no clergy-laity distinction
in the NT.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

How Does Paul's Mission Relate to Galatians?

- These two aspects of background material must be dealt with together because two opposing theories
of the identities of the recipients affect the dating of the letter. Both theories have logical weight and limited
biblical evidence.

- The two theories

- The traditional theory that was unanimous until the eighteenth century.

- It is called the "Northern Galatian Theory."

- It assumes that "Galatia" refers to the ethnic Galatians of the northern central plateau of Turkey
(cf. 1 Pet. 1:1). These ethnic Galatians were Celts (Greek Keltoi or Latin Gall) who
invaded this area in the third century B.C. They were called "Gallo-Graecians"
to distinguish them from their western European brothers. They were defeated in 230 B.C.
by Attalus I, the King of Pergamum. Their geographical influence was limited to northern central
Asia Minor or modern Turkey.

- If this ethnic group is assumed, then the date would be the mid 50's during Paul's second or third
missionary journey. Paul's traveling companions would be Silas and Timothy.

- Some have linked Paul's illness in Gal. 4:13 to malaria. They assert that Paul went north into the
highlands to get away from the marshy, malaria-infested, coastal lowlands.

- The second theory is championed by Sir Wm. M. Ramsay, St. Paul the Traveler and Roman Citizen,
New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1896.

- Whereas the traditional theory defined "Galatia" as ethnic, this theory defines it as administrative. It
seems that Paul often used Roman provincial names (cf. 1 Cor. 16:19; 2 Cor. 1:1; 8:1, etc.) The
Roman province of "Galatia" included a larger area than ethnic "Galatia." These ethnic Celts supported
Rome very early and were rewarded with more local autonomy and expanded territorial authority. If this
large area was known as "Galatia," then it is possible that Paul's first missionary journey to these
southern cities of Antioch in Pisidia, Lystra, Derbe and Iconium, recorded in Acts 13-14, is the location
of these churches.

- If one assumes this "Southern Theory," the date would be very early-close to, but before, the
"Jerusalem Council" of Acts 15, which addresses the same subject matter as the book of Galatians.
The Council occurred in A.D. 48-49 and the letter was probably written during the
same period. If this is true, Galatians is the first letter of Paul in our New Testament.

- Some evidences for the southern Galatian theory

(1) There is no mention of Paul's traveling companions by name, but Barnabas is
mentioned three times (cf. Gal. 2:1,9,13). This fits the first missionary journey of Paul.

(2) It is mentioned that Titus was not circumcised (cf. Gal. 2:1-5). This fits best
before the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

(3) The mention of Peter (cf. Gal. 2:11-14) and the problem of fellowship with
Gentiles fits best before the Jerusalem Council.

(4) When the money was taken to Jerusalem several companions of Paul from
different areas (cf. Acts 20:4) were listed. None, however, were listed from northern Galatia cities,
although we know these ethnic Galatian churches participated (cf. 1 Cor. 16:1). For a detailed
presentation of the different arguments concerning these theories, consult a technical commentary.
They each have valid points. At this point in time there is no consensus, but the "Southern Theory"
seems to fit all of the facts best.

- Relationship of Galatians to Acts

- Paul made five visits to Jerusalem, recorded by Luke in the book of Acts

- Acts 9:26-30, after his conversion

- Acts 11:22-30; 12:25, to bring famine relief from the Gentile churches

- Acts 15:1-30, the Jerusalem Council

- Acts 18:22, brief visit

- Acts 21:15ff, another defense of Paul's work among the Gentile areas to the Jerusalem church

- There are two visits to Jerusalem recorded in Galatians:

- Acts 1:18, after three years

- Acts 2:1, after fourteen years

- It seems most probable that Acts 9:26 is related to Gal. 1:18. Acts 11:30 and 15:1ff. are the setting of
unrecorded meetings which are mentioned in Gal. 2:1.

- There are some differences between the Acts 15 and Gal. 2 accounts but this is probably due to

- different perspectives

- different purposes of Luke and Paul

- the fact that Galatians 2 may have occurred sometime before the meeting described in
Acts 15 but in conjunction with it.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ACTS 14:1-7

1In Iconium they entered the synagogue of the Jews together, and spoke
in such a manner that a large number of people believed, both of Jews and of Greeks. 2But the Jews who disbelieved stirred
up the minds of the Gentiles and embittered them against the brethren. 3Therefore they spent a long time there speaking
boldly with reliance upon the Lord, who was testifying to the word of His grace, granting that signs and wonders be done by their hands.
4But the people of the city were divided; and some sided with the Jews, and some with the apostles. 5And when an
attempt was made by both the Gentiles and the Jews with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them, 6they became aware of it
and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding region; 7and there they continued to preach the gospel.
